interactions.label: A patient has a right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T10. Which combina

params.question: A patient has a right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T10. Which combination of sensory deficits is expected below the level of the lesion?

answers.text: Loss of pain and temperature on the right side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pain and temperature travel via the spinothalamic tract, which crosses within the spinal cord. A right-sided lesion therefore causes loss of pain and temperature on the opposite (left) side, not the same side.

answers.text: Loss of fine touch and proprioception on the left side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fine touch and proprioception ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway and cross only at the medulla. A right-sided cord lesion causes their loss on the right (same) side, not the left.

answers.text: Loss of fine touch on the right side and loss of pain sensation on the left side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In Brown-Séquard syndrome the DCML pathway (fine touch, proprioception) is interrupted ipsilaterally because it crosses in the medulla, while the spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) is interrupted contralaterally because it crosses within the cord.

answers.text: Bilateral loss of all sensations below the lesion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A hemisection damages only one side of the cord. Each sensory modality is lost on a different side because the two ascending tracts decussate at different levels — the hallmark of Brown-Séquard syndrome.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is that the two ascending pathways cross at different levels. The DCML crosses in the medulla, so its loss is ipsilateral. The spinothalamic tract crosses within the cord, so its loss is contralateral. This dissociated pattern defines Brown-Séquard syndrome.

Correct! Brown-Séquard syndrome produces ipsilateral loss of fine touch and proprioception (DCML crosses in the medulla) and contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic crosses within the cord).

interactions.label: Prostaglandins directly activate nociceptors to produce the sensation of pain.

params.question: Prostaglandins directly activate nociceptors to produce the sensation of pain.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Prostaglandins do not directly activate nociceptors. They lower the nociceptor firing threshold (sensitisation), making receptors more responsive to painful stimuli. Direct activation comes from mediators such as bradykinin and substance P. Aspirin blocks prostaglandin synthesis, thereby reducing sensitisation and pain.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done! Prostaglandins are sensitisers — they lower the threshold for nociceptor firing but do not directly activate nociceptors. Bradykinin and substance P are the direct activators. This is why aspirin, which blocks prostaglandin synthesis, reduces pain without being an anaesthetic.

interactions.label: In Parkinson's disease, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compac

params.question: In Parkinson's disease, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta degenerate. How does this produce the characteristic motor features?

answers.text: The direct pathway becomes overactive, causing involuntary choreiform movements

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dopamine loss actually reduces direct pathway activity. Overactivity of the direct (movement-facilitating) pathway is the mechanism in Huntington's disease, where the indirect pathway degenerates and the brake on movement is lost, producing chorea.

answers.text: The indirect pathway dominates, increasing thalamic inhibition and causing bradykinesia and rigidity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dopamine normally facilitates the direct pathway and suppresses the indirect pathway. When dopaminergic neurons are lost, the indirect pathway dominates, excessively inhibiting the thalamus and reducing motor cortex activation.

answers.text: Cerebellar output to the motor cortex is blocked, producing intention tremor and ataxia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Parkinson's disease affects the basal ganglia, not the cerebellum. It produces a resting tremor (present at rest, reduced by movement), whereas cerebellar lesions produce intention tremor and ataxia — signs on the same side as the lesion.

answers.text: Pyramidal tract fibres degenerate, producing spasticity and hyperreflexia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pyramidal (corticospinal) tract is intact in Parkinson's disease. Spasticity and hyperreflexia are upper motor neuron signs from pyramidal lesions. Parkinson's produces rigidity (lead-pipe or cogwheel type), which is an extrapyramidal sign.

overallFeedback.feedback: Dopamine normally facilitates movement via the direct pathway and suppresses the indirect pathway. When these neurons degenerate, the indirect pathway dominates — the thalamus is excessively inhibited, motor cortex activation falls, and the result is bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor.

Correct! Dopamine from the substantia nigra normally tips the balance toward the direct (movement-promoting) pathway. Its loss allows the indirect pathway to dominate, excessively suppressing thalamic output and producing bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor.

interactions.label: A patient with a thalamic stroke develops complete loss of sensation on the oppo

params.question: A patient with a thalamic stroke develops complete loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body, which later evolves into spontaneous burning pain on the same side. Which nucleus is most likely damaged, and what is this syndrome called?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The VPM nucleus relays face sensation and taste, not body sensation. Wallenberg syndrome is a lateral medullary (brainstem) stroke, not a thalamic lesion.
The LGN relays visual information to the primary visual cortex. Its damage causes visual field defects, not somatosensory loss or thalamic pain.

The VPL nucleus relays touch and pain from the body to the somatosensory cortex. Its damage causes contralateral sensory loss, followed during recovery by spontaneous, poorly localised burning pain — the hallmark of Déjerine-Roussy (thalamic pain) syndrome.

The VL nucleus relays cerebellar and basal ganglia output to the motor cortex. Its damage affects motor coordination, not sensation. Weber syndrome is a midbrain stroke causing oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is Déjerine-Roussy syndrome (thalamic pain syndrome). The VPL nucleus is the relay station for body sensation. Its damage first abolishes contralateral sensation, then produces spontaneous burning pain as recovery begins — a pattern specifically described in the narration.

Correct! Déjerine-Roussy syndrome results from VPL thalamic damage. Initial contralateral sensory loss is followed by the emergence of spontaneous, poorly localised thalamic pain that is characteristically resistant to treatment.

interactions.label: A 25-year-old patient presents with sudden, irresistible sleep attacks during th

params.question: A 25-year-old patient presents with sudden, irresistible sleep attacks during the daytime. Which neurotransmitter system, when lost, is most likely responsible?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Histaminergic neurons promote wakefulness, and their blockade by antihistamines causes drowsiness. However, loss of histaminergic neurons is not the specific cause of narcolepsy with its characteristic sudden sleep attacks.

Locus coeruleus neurons fire during waking and fall silent during REM sleep. Their dysfunction contributes to arousal deficits, but their selective loss does not produce the narcolepsy phenotype of sudden irresistible sleep.

Orexin neurons stabilise the waking state by reinforcing wake-promoting circuits. Their selective loss causes narcolepsy — the inability to maintain sustained wakefulness, with sudden transitions into sleep.

answers.text: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra are involved in motor control via the basal ganglia. Their degeneration causes Parkinson's disease (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia), not narcolepsy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Narcolepsy results from loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. These neurons stabilise wakefulness. Without them, the boundary between wake and sleep becomes unstable, producing sudden irresistible sleep attacks.
Correct! Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus stabilise the wake state. Their selective loss causes narcolepsy — sudden, irresistible transitions from wakefulness into sleep.

interactions.label: Which type of memory depends on the hippocampus for consolidation and is lost wh

params.question: Which type of memory depends on the hippocampus for consolidation and is lost when both hippocampi are damaged?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Procedural memory (motor skills and habits) depends on the basal ganglia and cerebellum, not the hippocampus. A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage can still perform learned motor skills such as riding a bicycle.

Declarative memory — the conscious recall of facts (semantic) and events (episodic) — requires hippocampal consolidation. Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia: the inability to form new declarative memories.

Classical conditioning relies on the cerebellum (for motor conditioning) and the amygdala (for fear conditioning), neither of which requires the hippocampus. These are forms of non-declarative memory.
Sensory memory lasts only milliseconds and operates at the level of sensory cortices. It does not require hippocampal processing and is not affected by hippocampal damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Declarative memory (conscious recall of facts and events) depends on the hippocampus. Non-declarative memory (skills, habits, conditioning) uses the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and amygdala instead, and is spared in hippocampal lesions.

Correct! Declarative memory (facts and events) requires hippocampal consolidation, occurring mainly during sleep. Bilateral hippocampal damage produces anterograde amnesia — new experiences cannot be stored as lasting memories.
